title: AI / LLM Systems (FDE-specific)
description: RAG, evaluation, guardrails, prompt engineering, LangChain/LangGraph, latency optimization. Critical for Turing FDE (LangChain/LangGraph is listed in the job req).

questions.prompt: In RAG, the 'retrieval' step returns:

options.text: Top-k semantically similar documents to include in the prompt

questions.explanation: RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Retrieve, then include in the LLM prompt as grounding context.

questions.prompt: Which chunking strategies are commonly used in RAG? (select all)

options.text: Semantic (split on sentence embeddings similarity drops)

questions.explanation: Fixed w/ overlap = baseline. Semantic = context-aware. Structural respects document layout. Very small or very large chunks perform poorly.

questions.prompt: Which favors RAG over fine-tuning?

options.text: Data changes daily and you need answers grounded in the latest state
You need the model to adopt a fixed style
You need fastest inference at any cost

questions.explanation: RAG = knowledge freshness + traceability + no retraining. Fine-tuning = style, structure, or domain reasoning where prompts alone don't reach. Prompt-engineer for one-off adjustments.

questions.prompt: 'LLM-as-judge' evaluation means:

options.text: Using another LLM to score outputs against a rubric or ground truth

questions.explanation: Judge-model produces score/preference. Watch for judge bias (position, verbosity, self-preference). Complement with human eval on stratified samples.

questions.prompt: Which are guardrail techniques for production LLMs? (select all)

options.text: Input allowlist / regex for known injection patterns
Output validation against a JSON schema
Trusting the system prompt to fully constrain behavior

questions.explanation: Layered defenses. Never trust the system prompt as sole enforcement — adversarial users bypass it.

questions.prompt: Defense-in-depth against prompt injection includes:

options.text: Isolating untrusted content in delimited sections + treating retrieved docs as data, not instructions

questions.explanation: Structured prompts, tool-use policies, least-privilege function calls, and output filtering. Injection is unsolved — assume some will get through.

questions.prompt: LangGraph differs from vanilla LangChain in that it:

options.text: Models agents as explicit state graphs with typed nodes/edges + persistence
Is a competitor with no interop

questions.explanation: LangGraph adds structured, resumable, observable graph execution — useful for real agent workflows Turing FDE listing calls out.

questions.prompt: Design a chunking strategy for a customer with mixed content (technical PDFs + Confluence pages + Slack export). Defend to a skeptical customer.

rubric.criterion: Different strategies per source type — no one-size-fits-all
Preserves structural boundaries (headings, code blocks, thread parents)
Keeps chunk-level metadata (source, path, timestamp, author) for filtering and citations
Overlap size chosen to preserve context without exploding index size
Plans an eval to compare strategies (recall@k against ground-truth Qs)
Frames the choice as testable, not dogmatic; commits to iteration

questions.modelAnswer: PDFs → structural chunk by heading, subchunk if > 800 tokens, 100-token overlap, keep page number metadata. Confluence → per-section with parent-title in metadata. Slack → one thread = one chunk, with thread parent + participant list as metadata. Every chunk carries {source_type, doc_id, path, updated_at, author}. Build a 50-question eval set from real user questions; measure recall@5 for each strategy; iterate.

questions.prompt: The customer says the model 'is getting worse.' No metrics exist. Plan the first 48 hours.

rubric.criterion: Clarifies: since when? Which task? Any recent changes (model version, prompt, data)?
Collects 20-50 concrete failing examples from the customer immediately
Establishes ground-truth eval set + baseline metric today (even simple exact match / thumbs)
Diffs: model version, prompt version, retrieval corpus deltas, upstream data drift
Interim mitigation (rollback prompt/model) while investigating
Written summary to customer within 24h with hypothesis + plan

questions.modelAnswer: Hour 0-4: get failing examples, timeline, changelogs. Hour 4-12: label eval set, run against current + previous model/prompt versions. Hour 12-24: identify regression source. Options — rollback prompt or model, patch retrieval, add filter. Hour 24-48: deploy fix + continuous eval, share written RCA outline with the customer.

questions.prompt: Which pushes you toward self-hosted LLMs vs a hosted API?

options.text: Data cannot leave the client VPC (compliance) OR very high sustained QPS
Small team, want to move fast

questions.explanation: Self-host is heavy — GPUs, ops, model updates. Choose when compliance or steady-state economics demand it.

questions.prompt: Design an end-to-end AI agent with tool use, memory, and evaluation, targeting 500 warehouse managers rerouting shipments with 99% delivery target.

rubric.criterion: Explicit tool definitions with typed schemas + auth per tool
Memory: short-term (conversation) + long-term (per-warehouse policies, previous decisions)
Human-in-the-loop for actions above impact threshold (dollar / customer)
Eval harness: replay decisions offline, compare to ground truth, track delivery rate KPI
Rollback / kill switch per warehouse
Observability: cost per decision, latency, tool failure rate

questions.modelAnswer: LangGraph agent: nodes = plan, retrieve context, propose reroute, get human approval if $ > $X, execute via SAP/WMS API. Short-term memory = message history. Long-term = per-warehouse Redis of {policies, priors}. Actions log to eventstore for replay. Nightly eval harness re-runs recent decisions against actual outcomes; compares proposed vs actual delivery rate. Rollout: shadow mode → 5 warehouses → 25 → all, with a per-warehouse toggle for instant kill.

questions.prompt: For a 50M-vector index with strict cost + on-prem needs, which is a reasonable default?

options.text: pgvector on Postgres with HNSW index

questions.explanation: pgvector with HNSW handles 10s of M vectors on beefy Postgres; Postgres already in the stack means less new infra. Above 100M, look at dedicated vector DBs (Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate).

questions.prompt: For a classification-style LLM task (extract-then-check), the strongest eval metric is:

options.text: Exact match / F1 against ground truth

questions.explanation: Match target format precisely — deterministic metrics before subjective ones. BLEU is for translation; perplexity for LM quality.

questions.prompt: First lever to cut LLM inference cost 5x without model swap?
questions.explanation: Exact-match cache is free. Semantic cache with an embedding lookup catches variants. After that: shorter prompts, smaller model for cheap tasks, prompt-caching APIs (Anthropic).

questions.prompt: Explain to a non-technical CFO why an LLM might produce different answers to the same input on different runs.

rubric.criterion: Uses a lay analogy without patronizing
Explains sampling / temperature in plain terms
States what CAN be made deterministic (temp=0, seed) and what can't (nondeterminism at hardware level)
Connects to business impact: report generation, audit, compliance
Offers a mitigation: guardrail + human review + logging every response

questions.modelAnswer: It's like asking a very fast writer to draft the same memo twice — same instructions, but a fresh draft with slightly different phrasing each time. We can turn 'creativity' down to nearly zero, so answers become very consistent, but two runs may still differ in small ways because the underlying math is nondeterministic on GPU hardware. For anything auditable, we log inputs and outputs, add automated checks on the output, and have a human sign off on critical decisions.

questions.prompt: An embedding for a piece of text is:

options.text: A fixed-length float vector positioned so that semantically similar texts are geometrically close

questions.explanation: Cosine or dot-product similarity in that vector space approximates semantic similarity.

questions.prompt: Which are common embedding model choices in 2026? (select all)
questions.explanation: LLMs like GPT-4 are generation models, not embedding models — different endpoints. Voyage, Mistral, Nomic are also popular.

questions.prompt: Choose pgvector over a dedicated vector DB when:

options.text: You already run Postgres, corpus is <10M vectors, and you want relational filtering next to embeddings without a separate service
You need >100M vectors and sub-10ms P99
You need cross-region replication for vectors

questions.explanation: pgvector = simplicity + JOIN with your relational data + one operational surface. Beyond ~10-50M, look at Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, or hosted Pinecone.

questions.prompt: HNSW vs IVF vector indexes — HNSW's trade-off:

options.text: Fastest at query time with great recall, higher memory footprint and slower build
Always faster than IVF at everything

questions.explanation: HNSW = graph-based, high recall, in-memory. IVF = clustering, less memory, needs training. pgvector supports both.

questions.prompt: Hybrid search means:

options.text: Combining dense (vector) + sparse (BM25/keyword) retrieval and fusing the ranks (e.g., Reciprocal Rank Fusion)

questions.explanation: Vector catches semantics; BM25 catches exact terms + rare vocab. RRF fuses lists without needing calibrated scores.

questions.prompt: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) improves retrieval by:

options.text: Asking the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer, embedding IT, and searching against that — often closer to real doc vectors than the raw question

questions.explanation: Trade-off: extra LLM call adds latency and cost; wins when questions are short/vague and docs are long/explicit.

questions.prompt: Cross-encoder reranker (Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker) in a RAG pipeline:

options.text: Retriever fetches top-k (e.g., 50); reranker scores each (query,doc) pair with more accuracy and picks top-n (e.g., 5) for the LLM

questions.explanation: Retriever = fast/approximate; reranker = slow/precise. Two-stage boosts relevance without exploding index cost.

questions.prompt: Which are RAGAS-style evaluation metrics? (select all)

options.text: Answer relevancy (does the answer address the question?)
Context recall (did we retrieve all needed docs?)

questions.explanation: RAGAS = 4 canonical metrics separating retrieval quality from generation quality. BLEU is a translation metric, not RAG-appropriate.

questions.prompt: Chain-of-Thought prompting:

options.text: Adds 'think step by step' or few-shot reasoning examples, encouraging the model to produce intermediate reasoning that improves final answers on math/logic tasks

questions.explanation: Newer 'thinking' models do this internally. For older/smaller models, explicit CoT still helps.

questions.prompt: Tool-calling (function-calling) requires the LLM to output:

options.text: Structured JSON matching a declared schema; the app parses + dispatches to the actual function; result is fed back for the next turn

questions.explanation: Use Pydantic (Python) / Zod (TS) to describe schemas. Model-native structured-output modes are more reliable than prompt-only JSON.

questions.prompt: The classic ReAct agent loop is:

options.text: Think (reason) → Act (call tool) → Observe (tool output) → repeat until answer or step limit

questions.explanation: LangGraph implements this as an explicit state graph with typed nodes/edges + persistence. Set max step count to bound cost.

questions.prompt: In LangGraph, checkpointing lets you:

options.text: Persist agent state per thread — resume interrupted runs, add human-in-the-loop approval, and time-travel to any prior step

questions.explanation: Checkpointers (Postgres, Redis, MemorySaver) enable durable multi-step agents. Essential for HITL.

questions.prompt: Anthropic/OpenAI prompt caching helps when:

options.text: A large stable prefix (system prompt + tool defs + long context) is reused across many turns — cached tokens cost less

questions.explanation: Design prompts so the stable part comes first, the variable part last. Big cost/latency win for RAG or long-conversation agents.

questions.prompt: Streaming tokens to a user improves:

options.text: Perceived latency (time-to-first-token drops dramatically) even though total tokens/sec is unchanged

questions.explanation: SSE from server → client. Also lets you display partial reasoning + stop early on user cancel.

questions.prompt: Which reduce hallucinations in production? (select all)

options.text: Ground with retrieved sources and require citations in the output
Refuse-to-answer if retrieval returns nothing above a similarity threshold
LLM-as-judge check for entailment against retrieved context
Add adversarial red-team eval to the CI harness

questions.explanation: Higher temperature INCREASES hallucination risk. Grounding + refusal + entailment checks + adversarial evals form the layered defense.

questions.prompt: Corrective RAG (CRAG) adds:

options.text: A retrieval evaluator that decides confidence in the docs; low-confidence triggers query rewrite or web search fallback

questions.explanation: Adaptive routing based on retrieval quality. Wins for open-domain Q&A.

questions.prompt: GraphRAG (Microsoft) differs from vector RAG in that it:

options.text: Uses graph databases as the store
Extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph, then does community summarization at query time — better for multi-hop, holistic questions

questions.explanation: Great when the answer needs to synthesize across many docs. Higher build cost. Hybrid graph+vector is common.

questions.prompt: Long-context models (1M+ tokens) don't fully replace RAG because:

options.text: Cost scales with tokens, attention degrades over very long inputs ('needle in haystack' failures), and retrieval offers auditability/citation

questions.explanation: Long-context + RAG is often the best combo. Cost per token quickly dominates when you stuff full docs.

questions.prompt: For multi-tenant RAG, per-tenant isolation is best enforced by:

options.text: One shared index, trust the LLM to respect tenant boundaries
Metadata filter on tenant_id at the vector-DB level applied BEFORE the LLM sees any doc

questions.explanation: Never rely on the LLM to filter. Enforce at retrieval. For very sensitive tenants: per-tenant index (physical isolation).

questions.prompt: Indirect prompt injection is:

options.text: Malicious instructions hidden in RETRIEVED documents (or tool outputs) that the LLM then follows

questions.explanation: Any content brought in from outside the system prompt is untrusted. Mitigations: mark data explicitly, output filtering, capability limits on tools.

questions.prompt: Best control against tool-call abuse in an agentic system:

options.text: Least-privilege tools + policy layer that authorizes each tool call against the requesting user's permissions BEFORE execution

questions.explanation: Treat tools like an API surface: authz, audit, rate limits, scoped credentials. Never trust the model to enforce authz.

questions.prompt: Design a golden-eval + regression suite for a RAG system before you launch it to a customer.

rubric.criterion: Curates 50-200 real questions with expected answers + expected retrieved doc IDs
Splits into categories: factual lookup, multi-hop, ambiguous, out-of-scope (refuse), adversarial (injection)
Automates: retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR) + generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, exact-match where possible)
Runs on every prompt/model/chunking change; gates PRs on non-regression
Includes cost + latency in the report
Includes a human review pipeline for a random sample

questions.modelAnswer: Pair with 2 domain experts to draft 100 questions across the 5 categories. Store as YAML with (question, expected_answer, expected_doc_ids, category, difficulty). Nightly job runs retrieval + generation, computes RAGAS metrics + custom exact-match. Post to dashboard + Slack. CI blocks PRs with regressions >5% on any category. Sample 10 random runs to a human reviewer weekly for calibration.

questions.prompt: Design a LangGraph agent that answers customer-support tickets by (a) classifying intent, (b) looking up account data, (c) drafting a reply, (d) requesting human approval for refunds > $100.

rubric.criterion: State schema: ticket, intent, account, draft, needs_approval, decision
Nodes for each step; edges include conditional routing on intent + needs_approval
Tool definitions for account lookup (typed input/output)
Human-in-the-loop via checkpointer interrupt; agent resumes after approval
Guardrails: max step count, PII redaction on logging, refund cap enforced by policy layer not just prompt
Observability + eval hook per node

questions.modelAnswer: State: `{ ticket, intent, account, draft, refund_amount, approval_needed, decision }`. Nodes: classify → lookup → draft → check_amount (conditional edge: if refund > $100 → interrupt for human else send). Checkpointer = Postgres. Tools: `get_account(user_id)` (typed via Zod). Policy layer wraps `send_refund(amount)` — throws if > $100 without approval token. Max 6 steps. All state logs redact PII. Langfuse traces every node.

questions.prompt: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning:

options.text: Adds small rank-decomposition matrices to attention layers, training only those (millions of params vs billions) — cheap + composable

questions.explanation: LoRA adapters can be swapped per task. QLoRA quantizes the base model to 4-bit for even lower cost.

questions.prompt: For self-hosted LLM inference, high-throughput stack is typically:

options.text: vLLM or TGI + continuous batching + KV-cache reuse + tensor parallelism on multi-GPU

questions.explanation: vLLM's PagedAttention manages KV-cache like virtual memory — dramatic throughput gains over naive serving.

questions.prompt: 4-bit quantization (GPTQ, AWQ) trades:

options.text: ~4x smaller memory + faster inference for a small accuracy drop (usually <1% on benchmarks) — enables big models on smaller GPUs

questions.explanation: 8-bit ≈ nearly lossless. 4-bit is the current sweet spot for serving 70B models on a single 48GB GPU.

questions.prompt: Getting reliable JSON output from an LLM: best pattern:

options.text: Use model-native structured-output / JSON mode with a Zod/Pydantic schema; retry on parse failure with the error message included in the retry prompt

questions.explanation: Anthropic tool-use, OpenAI structured outputs, and Gemini schemas all enforce validity. Zod/Pydantic gives you client-side validation + TypeScript inference.

questions.prompt: In an LLM app, primary cost driver you should dashboard first:

options.text: Input + output tokens per request, broken down by endpoint + user cohort — reveals runaway prompts / high-cost users

questions.explanation: Log tokens_in / tokens_out / model / user_id / cost_estimate per call. Alert on outliers. This one dashboard prevents 80% of surprise-bill incidents.

questions.prompt: The most COMMON RAG failure mode in production is:

options.text: Retrieval misses the right document (poor chunking / query mismatch) — retrieval quality is the ceiling on answer quality

questions.explanation: If retrieval doesn't return the right passage, no LLM can save you. Invest in retrieval evaluation first, generation second.

questions.prompt: A RAG API's P95 latency is 3.2s. Target: 1s. Walk through your reduction plan.

rubric.criterion: Break down latency: embed + retrieve + rerank + LLM (with TTFT) + network
Add semantic-cache on the full-question level (huge saving on FAQ traffic)
Stream tokens to reduce perceived latency even if total unchanged
Use a smaller/faster model for easy questions with a router
Colocate services + use prompt-caching for the stable prefix
Batch or parallelize embed + retrieve + rerank where possible
Set explicit SLOs + regression alerts

questions.modelAnswer: Profile P95 breakdown. Add exact-match + semantic-cache first (biggest lever for FAQ). Route easy intents to a fast small model; hard to the big one. Enable prompt caching on the system prompt + tool defs. Stream tokens. If retrieval is 400ms, precompute embeddings + move vector DB into the same VPC/az. Parallelize the rerank with early-cut. Commit to per-endpoint SLOs and alert on burn.
